The billboard rotates every few seconds on its slats between three adverts: a film poster for the stories, a newsreader ad for the bulletin, and a hi-vis political campaign poster for the Government. Each advert is a fully designed poster with a tagline in a different typeface. The visitor can scroll to rotate the board by hand or tap a pole-mounted control box (a grey junction box with three buttons) to pick one. Between rotations, the three slats briefly show the whole site's tagline in fragments.
ideas.strands: Face 1 (stories) is a matte, cinematic, dark poster with film-grain and a pull-quote; Face 2 (news) is a hard red-and-white broadcast ident with a ticker along the bottom; Face 3 (the party) is a flat yellow-and-black campaign poster with a rosette and a large plain-English promise. When the slats turn, the whole surrounding scene's light shifts to match the face (night cinema, studio fluorescent, daylight). The logo ring is bolted on top of the billboard like a lamp.
ideas.hero: First 5 seconds: a lay-by at dusk, lorries passing, and the billboard slats snap round with a clatter from an advert for 'BADCODE' to three distinct posters, ending on a cheerful one that says 'THE FUTURE HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. IT WAS RUBBISH.' The camera pushes slowly toward the board.
ideas.reader_fit: A trivision on a retail-park roundabout is the most British piece of public advertising there is. It says 'we are an ordinary thing you pass on the way home', not 'we are an art project'. Posters are the native language of UK politics, the Saturday-night telly and the cinema.
ideas.risk: A rotating sign is passive, so the visitor may wait for the next face rather than choosing, and slats can reduce legibility on mobile. It needs a clear manual control, and a 'seen it, jump' fast path so a returning visitor is never made to wait.

lens: Live data and receipts: tickers, clocks, counters and trackers that make a homepage feel alive and accountable every day. Eight searches were run, and I did not fetch any pages. Where I could not verify a design detail, the reference says so.

references.name: Climate Clock, Union Square (Golan and Boyd, 2020)
references.what: A civic clock built from a real one. The Metronome was turned into a public countdown to the carbon-budget deadline, in red. A second green number, the 'lifeline', shows renewable share. Artists Gan Golan and Andrew Boyd cite the Doomsday Clock and the National Debt Clock as influences.
references.steal: Two numbers in opposite colours that race each other: a red 'deadline' against a green 'lifeline'. The page reads as a duel and the viewer works out who is winning. We could run one pair per strand. The mounted-on-a-building feel, a giant digital sign bolted over something ordinary, is also worth stealing.

references.name: Wealth, Shown to Scale (Matt Korostoff, 1-pixel-wealth)
references.what: A scroll site where one pixel is $1,000. You scroll a long, empty page past ordinary wealth figures to reach a billionaire's fortune, one screen at a time. Mirrors and classroom versions exist, for example https://oadouglas.github.io/Wealth-To-Scale-Adapted-For-Classroom. The author is Korostoff, not neal.fun.
references.steal: The joke is the effort. Scroll distance is the argument. A homepage where one tiny row stands for a nurse's weekly pay and the scrolling takes forever to reach the first tick of a chairman's pay needs no caption. The page proves the point by being tedious.

references.name: US debt clock sites (us-debt-clock.com and similar)
references.what: Dense walls of fast-ticking dollar figures with per-citizen and per-taxpayer breakdowns. A forum page shows a $39.69 trillion figure with the note 'Algorithmically projected from latest Treasury data'. Another clone, USDebtClock.co, names the Treasury Fiscal Data API as its source and interpolates each second from a 30-day average growth rate. I could not retrieve usdebtclock.org's own page, so its exact layout is unverified.
references.steal: Honest fakery. The ticking is a projection from the latest real figure, and the footnote says so. This is a good model for our 'money found this week' counter: it ticks live, and the small print gives the source and the method. The per-person divisor ('per household', 'per nurse') is the other steal.

references.name: Doomsday Clock, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists
references.what: One hand and one number, reset by a committee about once a year. It stood at 90 seconds to midnight in 2023 and at 89 seconds in the January announcement described here. The range runs from 17 minutes in 1991 to 89 seconds.
references.steal: A rare, ceremonial update with a long history strip behind it. A homepage 'dial' that moves only when BadCode rules on it, with every past setting kept, would turn the live-data idea into an event. Seven minutes to midnight in 1947 and 89 seconds now is a ready-made archive timeline.

references.name: TheyWorkForYou (mySociety)
references.what: A UK charity's parliamentary monitor. It covers Hansard for the Commons, Lords, Scottish Parliament and NI Assembly, with voting records, the Register of Members' Interests, an API and RSS. Every section has a permalink. Commons debates go back to 1918.
references.steal: The receipt is a permalink to the real record. Each BadCode Government claim could carry a small link to the Hansard passage it answers. Because the data is open, the cabinet's own words can be pulled in as a live feed. The visual tone is plain public-record paper, which carries more weight than slickness.

references.name: Worldometer
references.what: A homepage of live counters whose numbers roll as change unfolds. Its About page says they are generated by a proprietary real-time estimate algorithm drawing on official sources. A review calls the layout basic, mostly tables, graphs and numbers. I could not confirm how it animates the digits.
references.steal: A wall of unrelated counters that all move at once and make the page feel like a control room. Plain styling is part of the authority. Counter rows named for our own jokes ('Nurses: £0', 'Consultancy fees this hour') would make the same wall funny.

references.name: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires
references.what: A ranked list that updates with the market. A 2014 launch article says public holdings are revalued about every 5 minutes while markets are open and private holdings once a day. That cadence may have changed. Bloomberg's index, by contrast, is a daily close-of-day ranking and not a true ticker (https://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/).
references.steal: A leaderboard whose rows shuffle position as the numbers move. A ranked table of 'who got paid this week' with arrows and rank changes makes the news strand look like a league table. Bloomberg's daily-close rhythm suggests a ceremonial 'closing bell' each evening.

references.name: Split-flap displays and LAb[au] 'Signal To Noise'
references.what: The clattering mechanical departure board. LAb[au]'s installation uses 512 recycled split-flaps to turn data into sound and pattern. The Wikipedia entry is at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Split-flap_display.
references.steal: A UK railway departures board is the one object every working-class Brit has stared at in the cold. Use flipping letters, with the clatter as sound, for the strand names and for headlines. It is tactile, familiar and not crypto.

ideas.name: DEPARTURES
ideas.concept: The homepage is a full-viewport railway station departures board in black enamel, amber and off-white split-flap letters. It has the clatter, the slightly stiff flips and a scuffed bezel. Every row is a 'service' leaving from BadCode. The board re-flips every few seconds with real, dated content. 'Platform' is the strand, 'Status' is a live receipt ('DELAYED: Nurses, 0 days since last pay rise'), and 'Calling at' lists the contents. A BadCode Government row shows 'Today's manifesto: 14 changes, 1 contradicts the Chancellor, 0 apologies'. Clicking a row opens that strand. The ring-and-triangle eye sits as the station clock above the board, and its triangle is the second hand.
ideas.strands: Three platforms, three row families. Platform 1 STORIES in off-white with a film-and-song glyph, rows are the four stories and eight videos, status is 'RUNNING' or 'NOW SHOWING'. Platform 2 BULLETIN is amber and flips fastest because it is the topical one, with rows that are headlines, the 'Nurses: £0' tally and 'money found this week'. Platform 3 GOVERNMENT is a slower, heavier row in the logo red, with manifesto lines struck through when the real cabinet contradicts them. The platform number and the speed of the flip tell them apart, and the sound does too: stories clack slowly, news clacks nonstop, government gives one heavy thunk.
ideas.hero: On load the board is blank and silent. For one beat it is pitch black with only the eye-clock. Then the whole board clatters into life, hundreds of flaps at once, settling letter by letter from left to right until the three platform names land: STORIES, BULLETIN, GOVERNMENT. A single red row flips last: 'NEXT DEPARTURE: 00:03:12', counting down to the next bulletin drop. Tap the screen and the sound can be toggled.
ideas.reader_fit: Everyone in the UK has stood under a departures board in the cold and been told 'delayed' with no explanation. It borrows the language of a service that does not work and flips it. A board is plain, municipal and not slick, and it carries authority without condescension. Nothing about it reads as crypto, tech bro or activist.
ideas.risk: The board is a metaphor that could swallow the content. Rows are small text, so the films and the music have no visual room, and a station gimmick fades after the first visit. Mitigate by letting each row expand into a window onto the strand. The sound must default to off. Real accessibility work is needed too, because flipping text is hard to read for some people.

ideas.name: THE SCALE OF IT
ideas.concept: The homepage borrows Wealth, Shown to Scale and makes the scroll the whole identity. The first screen is a tall, nearly empty field of cream paper with one tiny red triangle at the top and a ruler down the left edge in pounds. As you scroll, the page unrolls through a long strip where one pixel equals a fixed sum. The three strands are three markers on the strip, each placed at the amount of money it is about. The strip runs through a nurse's yearly pay, then a household bill, then a consultancy fee, a ministerial contract, and a billionaire's fortune, with BadCode's three doors cut into the paper at those points. The ruler is the navigation, and a live counter in the corner shows how far you have scrolled in pounds and in minutes of your own life.
ideas.strands: Each strand sits at a different altitude on the ruler. STORIES is at the human end, near a nurse's annual salary, drawn as a lit window with a thumbnail of each film. The BULLETIN sits mid-way at the figure of the week's story (a hospital contract, a consultancy bill), and its number changes daily, so the page grows or shrinks on every visit. GOVERNMENT sits at the far end, where the page has become a mile of blank paper, with a single door that opens only after a long scroll. Colour changes with depth: warm cream and ink at the bottom, then pale grey, then white with a hard red rule. A fast-scrolling 'skip' button exists because the tedium is the point but should not be a trap.
ideas.hero: The first five seconds are quiet. The red triangle drifts down the page on its own, and a caption in small caps types out: 'This is a nurse's year, to scale.' It is one pixel high. The page scrolls itself a few hundred pixels, then stops, and a sentence says 'The next door is ten thousand times further.' The viewer realises the page is a measuring tape before any menu appears.
ideas.reader_fit: It makes the point the reader already feels in their own bank balance without telling them what to think, which respects the rule never to say 'you've been duped'. The reader does the arithmetic. It also uses ordinary sums in pounds, such as a nurse's wage and a household bill, and avoids billionaire-bashing as the opening move.
ideas.risk: It is a one-trick page that people recognise from the original and from copies, so it may feel borrowed. Long scrolls hurt on mobile and hide the three strands from anyone who does not scroll. The fix is a fixed three-door nav strip always visible at the bottom, and a clear credit to the idea. The figures must be sourced and dated, since a wrong sum on a page about receipts is fatal.

ideas.name: THE RACE
ideas.concept: The page is a live duel between two numbers in the manner of the Climate Clock's red deadline and green lifeline, scaled up to fill the whole screen. On the left, in hard red, is 'what they said': a ticking count of days since the last promise, pounds announced, pounds delivered. On the right, in a warm sodium-lamp yellow, is 'what we filed': BadCode's manifesto lines, receipts and bulletins. The two columns run like a split-screen sports scoreboard with enormous seven-segment digits. In between sits the eye of the logo as a referee. Beneath the scoreboard the three strands appear as three 'commentary boxes', each with a live feed. Numbers are projected from the latest real figure and labelled as projections, in the manner of the debt clocks.
ideas.strands: The scoreboard is the umbrella, and the three strands are the three commentary boxes beneath it. STORIES is a dark box with a looping film poster and a small 'Now showing' tag, the one place the scoreboard goes quiet. BULLETIN is a news-ticker strip that crawls along the bottom of the whole screen, always moving, with the presenter's red-triangle eyepatch silhouette in a corner. GOVERNMENT is the manifesto column itself, a daily-updating list in the yellow half, each line with a small Hansard link as its receipt. Typography separates them: seven-segment for numbers, a heavy grotesque for the bulletin, a typewriter face for the manifesto.
ideas.hero: The screen opens as a stadium scoreboard powering on: the digits flick through 8s and settle. The left number is 'DAYS SINCE PROMISE: 1,204' in red, the right number is 'LINES FILED TODAY: 14' in yellow, and a hard buzzer-like tick marks each second. The referee eye blinks once, and a caption reads 'Same news. Opposite conclusions. Receipts kept.' The tick sound is the only audio and it is muted until the viewer chooses.
ideas.reader_fit: A scoreboard is the football-terrace language of a pub, readable at a glance and fair-minded in form: two sides, one score, receipts. It does not preach. It also lets the reader decide who is winning, which is the opposite of condescension.
ideas.risk: Fabricated or stale numbers are the main danger. A page about receipts with one wrong figure loses its point, so every counter needs a source line and an 'estimated' flag. A two-column duel also pushes the storytelling strand to the margin, and on narrow phones the split-screen has to stack. Finally, the richer the live feed, the more daily maintenance it demands from two people, so the first version should run from a single JSON file written by the Government agents.

lens: Contrarian creative coding: make the homepage behave like a machine that has already seen how it ends. Eyes, terminals, git history, tape decay and net-art rule-breaking, rather than a tidy brand site.

references.name: WebGazer.js (Brown HCI)
references.what: Browser JS that turns a webcam into a rough eye tracker, with calibration. It runs entirely client-side.
references.steal: Don't actually use the webcam (creepy, permission wall, and wrong for this reader). Steal the idea of a gaze: the logo-eye finds where YOU are looking and the page reacts. A mouse/touch proxy is enough, since research shows cursor position correlates closely with gaze.

references.name: Framer 'Cursor Eye Mascot' / three.js eye-follow components
references.what: Pupils that track the cursor across the whole viewport, some WebGL versions with eyelid squints that respond to cursor distance.
references.steal: Pupil tracking across the whole viewport with an eyelid squint as the cursor gets close. Here the pupil is the red triangle, rotating to point at you and narrowing the ring like an eyelid.

references.name: term-website / Termfolio (xterm.js)
references.what: A site that is a real shell: tab completion, history, URL routes that auto-run commands (visiting /projects runs `cd projects && ls`).
references.steal: Routes as commands. Each strand is a command that runs on load (`git log --stories`, `tail -f news`, `cat manifesto`), and the nav is a prompt the visitor can also type into, with big tap-targets for people who won't.

references.name: Gource
references.what: OpenGL visualisation of a repo's history as a growing tree: directories are branches, files are leaves, contributors are avatars flying about and committing.
references.steal: The tree growing out of one root and then forking is the BadCode origin myth already. Render it as a time-lapse of the world's history, with the bad branch dying and the good branch (Future Proof) sprouting into daylight.

references.name: CRTFilter (WebGL library)
references.what: WebGL post-process with barrel distortion, scanlines, dot mask, flicker and VHS tracking artefacts.
references.steal: A rolling tracking bar and tape jitter as a whole-page layer. Tune each strand's amount of decay: lots on News (it is a transmission), none on Future Proof (clean daylight).

references.name: Spectral 3D ghost effect (three.js + GLSL, FreeFrontend)
references.what: Mouse-tracking entity with time-quantised jitter, VHS glitch and bloom in a custom shader pass.
references.steal: Time-quantised jitter (it snaps on 12fps steps rather than smoothly), which feels like tape damage instead of a digital shimmer. The pattern would also fit a masked news-host silhouette that follows the cursor.

references.name: JODI, wwwwwwwww.jodi.org (1995)
references.what: Net-art landmark that deliberately breaks the layout: letter noise, error text and a maze of dead ends that turns out to be readable source.
references.steal: Make the break part of the joke. Source code or a 'error: timeline diverged' message leaks out of the page, and a small number of readable truths are buried in the noise (the receipts).

references.name: Bruno Simon's drivable portfolio (Awwwards SOTM Nov 2019)
references.what: Three.js world where you drive a car between project signs with keyboard or touch.
references.steal: Proof that a visitor will play with a homepage if the controls take one second to learn. The lesson is a single verb for the whole site, not a drivable 3D world.

references.name: Buck sandbox: moshing
references.what: Studio experiment in datamoshing: motion vectors from one clip drag pixels from another.
references.steal: A transition that smears one strand's footage into the next, so scrolling from Stories to News looks like the video codec has failed. The history is bleeding through.

ideas.name: THE GAZE
ideas.concept: The whole homepage is one enormous logo-eye on a near-black field: a thin ring the size of the viewport, with a red triangle pupil. The pupil tracks your cursor or finger, rotating to face you, and the ring narrows like an eyelid as you get close. Dragging the pupil toward a region of the ring is how you choose. The ring is split in three arcs, each a strand, and scrolling pushes you through the iris into that strand. The eye behaves as though it already knows which one you'll pick. Idle for 4 seconds and it picks for you, with a deadpan caption.
ideas.strands: The ring is divided into three arcs at 10, 2 and 6 o'clock. Top-left arc (STORIES) is warm projector flicker with film-gate sprocket marks and tiny poster thumbnails drifting in it. Right arc (NEWS) is a sickly broadcast blue-grey, with a lower-third ticker running round the arc itself and a pulsing 'Nurses: £0' counter. Bottom arc (GOVERNMENT) is the one lit place: flat, bright, building-site hi-vis yellow-green (#d8e24a) against black, with a plain stencil crest. Pupil hovering an arc floods the ring-interior with that strand's live content, like the eye is reading it.
ideas.hero: Black screen. A thin white ring draws itself in, then the red triangle snaps in, off-centre at 2 o'clock, and swivels to the exact pixel of your cursor. It holds there for a beat and then a single deadpan line types underneath: 'You were going to click that.' Then the three arcs light up in sequence.
ideas.reader_fit: No explaining or lecturing, just a gimmick that's a laugh within a second and works with a thumb on a phone (tilt/touch replaces the mouse). The sarcasm makes the visitor feel noticed, not studied, and the three strands are plain-worded: Stories, News, Government.
ideas.risk: Only the eye is memorable and the three destinations can feel like thin portals. A cursor-follow eye is also a familiar cliche (mascot widgets), so the unusual part, the eyelid and arc selection, has to be built well and run smoothly on a cheap Android.

ideas.name: git log --all --graph
ideas.concept: The homepage is a live terminal, black with pure white monospace and the logo's red used only for the cursor block and for HEAD. On load it runs `git log --graph --all` and prints an ASCII branch history that is the lore: a long bad branch running to a dead end labelled 'humanity: removed', and a branch forking off it. Commits are scrollable and clickable and each commit message is a piece of content (a film, a bulletin, a policy). A prompt at the bottom accepts typing (`help`, `news`, `vote`, `sudo undo`), and every command also exists as a big tap button above it for people who will never type.
ideas.strands: Three long-lived branches checked out in parallel, each in its own column of the graph: `stories/` (commits are films and songs, hash-style IDs like 'a3f9 Karen Will Lead the Revolution'), `news/` (a commit per bulletin, newest at the top, pushed daily, with the 'Nurses: £0' tally as a CI status badge that stays red), and `government/` (the only branch with a green 'passing' build and a merged pull request called future-proof). Each branch has its own text colour: amber for stories, white for news, and an unnatural bright green for government.
ideas.hero: Black screen, a cursor blinks, and in 5 seconds a real git graph prints itself line by line: the bad branch grows to a dead end with `* 2054  (bad-timeline) humanity: removed` in red, and a fork is drawn with a single `|\` that opens into three branches. A final line: `$ git checkout -b better`.
ideas.reader_fit: Dead plain, no jargon you can't skim past. It is a printed record and receipts, which reads as honest to a reader who distrusts polish, and the dry authority is the narrator's voice. The risk to guard is reading as 'developer in-joke', so every commit message is written in plain pub English.
ideas.risk: It is a terminal-portfolio cliche (see Termfolio/CLIfolio) and risks reading as a programmer's site, not a working-class UK one. Mitigation: the typed prompt is optional garnish, the buttons do all the work, and the lore is in the graph, not the jargon.

ideas.name: THE SIGNAL
ideas.concept: The homepage is a television that is picking up three channels from a broken future. A full-screen CRT/VHS shader (barrel curve, scanlines, rolling tracking bar, tape jitter snapped to 12fps) sits over the page, and a tuner dial at the bottom is the nav. Turning it is dragging, or tapping the channel numbers 1, 2, 3. Between channels it datamoshes: the previous channel's footage smears into the next one along motion vectors, and static briefly spells readable truths. The set's reception is driven by the visitor's real clock: late evening gets deeper static and a 'broadcasting from 2054' caption, daytime is cleaner.
ideas.strands: CH 1 STORIES: letterboxed film, grainy, warm, projecting a looping scrap of the current films as thumbnails on a 'VHS shelf' strip, with film sprocket holes down the edges. CH 2 NEWS: the broadcast, with a picture-in-picture of the masked host (white balaclava, red-triangle eyepatch, never speaking) and a scrolling lower-third ticker plus the 'Nurses: £0' tally in a chunky seven-segment display. CH 3 GOVERNMENT: the only clean channel, with all CRT effects fading to zero: flat daylight, hi-vis yellow on pale concrete grey, plain sans type, a hoarding sign reading 'FUTURE PROOF: BUILDING' that overwrites the static, the sole lit place in the set.
ideas.hero: The screen is dead grey static. A tuner clunks, the picture rolls vertically once, and the tracking bar settles on the ring-and-triangle logo, which is the idle channel, with the triangle blinking like a standby light. After 3 seconds it dissolves in a datamosh smear into CH 2, the news, and the host's lower-third reads 'WE HAVE SEEN THIS BULLETIN BEFORE.'
ideas.reader_fit: Everyone knows the TV, and the point lands without a word of politics: the news is broken, here's a channel that isn't. It's nostalgic and tactile, works on a phone, and the 'bad reception' joke is familiar from every 90s living room, so it feels like theirs. The Government channel being the only clean picture says the thing without a sermon.
ideas.risk: Heavy shader passes will struggle on cheap phones and can hurt legibility and accessibility (flicker, motion). It needs a reduced-motion and low-power fallback that keeps the look as static CSS, and the retro-VHS aesthetic is itself widely overused, so execution has to be unusually specific to BadCode.
